summary: The Arar crossing between Iraq and Saudi Arabia was closed to ordinary commercial trade in 1990 after relations broke down following Iraq’s invasion of Kuwait. The countries formally reopened it for trade on 18 November 2020 as relations improved. Pilgrims had been allowed through during the intervening years, so the trade restriction did not mean that every form of passage stopped.

verification.notes: Retained year-only onset and formal trade permission; pilgrimage access distinguished.

summary: Iraqi authorities closed the Trebil–Karameh crossing with Jordan in July 2015 during the conflict with Islamic State, partly to prevent the group collecting money from road traffic. Officials held a reopening ceremony on 30 August 2017, and loaded commercial trucks were crossing by 4 October. Temporary clearances occurred during the restriction, and neither the first normal freight passage nor the restoration of ordinary passenger travel is precisely dated.

verification.notes: Used current July onset bounds and actual cargo-by-October evidence; ceremony not treated as operational endpoint.

summary: Jordan closed the Jaber–Nassib crossing with Syria on 31 March 2015 because fighting between Syrian government forces and rebels had approached the crossing. Civilian passengers were observed crossing again on 15 October 2018, following the Syrian government’s recovery of the surrounding area. Trucks carrying Syrian produce also entered Jordan later that day, while Syrian travellers remained subject to security clearance.

verification.notes: Passenger onset and reopening supported; later same-day directional freight distinguished.

summary: Saudi Arabia closed its Salwa–Abu Samra border with Qatar in June 2017 during the diplomatic dispute in which it accused Qatar of supporting extremism and maintaining ties with Iran; Qatar rejected the allegations. Ordinary passenger vehicles returned on 9 January 2021, followed by commercial traffic on 14 February. Pilgrimage and humanitarian exceptions had allowed some earlier passage, so the episode was not an uninterrupted ban on every traveller and shipment.

verification.notes: Preserved June onset uncertainty, attributed allegations, exceptional passage and separate passenger/freight endings.

summary: Fighting between Hayat Tahrir al-Sham and Ahrar al-Sham disrupted the Syrian approach to Bab al-Hawa in July 2017. Armed roadblocks stopped aid and commercial trucks arriving from Turkey from 19 July, with freight passage reported again on 26 July after ceasefire arrangements. The documented interruption concerns the approach road and incoming freight; the timing of passenger restrictions is less clear.

verification.notes: Separated armed approach-road blockade from Turkish maintenance; freight-only dated phase.

summary: Iran’s main official crossings with Iraqi Kurdistan stopped ordinary trade and passenger movement on 15 October 2017, according to Kurdish customs officials, who linked the action to Baghdad’s response to the independence referendum. Iran initially denied imposing new measures. Bashmakh reportedly reopened on 25 October, while trade and passenger movement at Parwezkhan and Haji Omaran resumed on 2 January 2018. Waiting travellers and the semi-official Tawqela route were initially excepted.

verification.notes: Kept disputed attribution, three gate-specific endpoints and exceptions.

summary: Passenger movement at al-Wadea, between Yemen and Saudi Arabia, stopped briefly on 8 November 2017 and resumed the same day. Local reporting described a roughly two-hour interruption, with a crossing employee referring to legal procedures. Although it followed the Saudi-led coalition’s wider blockade announcement, the evidence does not establish that this short stoppage implemented that order; subsequent reports described normal passenger and commercial traffic.

verification.notes: Corrected inherited supplies-only framing using accepted passenger phase; ordering actor and motive not assumed.

summary: Iraqi authorities announced a 24-hour closure of the country’s land crossings around the parliamentary election on 12 May 2018, presenting it as a security measure. Reports differ over whether the closure was to begin at noon on 11 May or around midnight. The available accounts describe the order but do not establish the actual closing and reopening times at individual land crossings.

verification.notes: Presented an announced 24-hour order; conflicting schedules not combined into a longer observed closure.

summary: Pakistan suspended travel and trade at Taftan–Mirjaveh in late February 2020 to limit the spread of COVID-19 from Iran. Pakistani pilgrims and other citizens were being admitted from Iran by 28 February, subject to screening and quarantine. Commercial trucks began passing again on 7 March under health controls; later changes to trading schedules were separate restrictions, rather than the end of this initial stoppage.

verification.notes: Kept late-February onset bounds and distinct returnee/cargo reopening dates.

summary: Türkiye restricted road arrivals from Iran on 23 February 2020 to prevent COVID-19 transmission, while permitting screened returns by Turkish citizens and some controlled exports. Freight arrangements changed gradually, including unaccompanied rail wagons, exceptional truck entry and renewed freight permission at Gürbulak on 4 June 2020. Ordinary day-trip pedestrians were observed using Gürbulak–Bazargan again on 8 October 2021; that date does not establish reopening at every Turkish–Iranian crossing.

verification.notes: Distinguished freight exceptions and formal permission from observed Gürbulak pedestrian return.

summary: Commercial freight stopped at Shushme–Shushmi, between Iran and Iraqi Kurdistan, during the COVID-19 restrictions of February 2020. Reuters filmed trucks crossing again on 3 May and quoted an employee dating the closure to 28 February. Other reports give a 25 February start and an opening on 28 April, leaving the exact duration uncertain; the evidence does not establish when passenger travel resumed.

verification.notes: Preserved contradictory onset and reopening reports; avoided continuous precise duration.

summary: Saudi Arabia restricted its citizens’ ordinary overseas travel in March 2020 as part of its COVID-19 response, including departures through land crossings. Specified official, employment, business, medical and student journeys were permitted from September 2020. Wider travel permission returned on 17 May 2021 for citizens meeting health requirements, with subsequent departures reported at several land posts; the change did not remove every condition on travel.

verification.notes: Outward citizen leisure policy distinguished from exempt categories and all-border physical closure.

summary: Jordan restricted ordinary passenger travel through its land crossings in March 2020 to contain COVID-19, while commercial freight, some diplomatic travel and necessary returns by Jordanians remained permitted. By 29 October, Al-Mudawwarah, King Hussein Bridge and Sheikh Hussein Bridge had reopened to approved passengers under quotas. This was a partial restoration at three crossings; the first passenger movements and the reopening of other posts are not established.

verification.notes: March land start kept imprecise; three-post quota reopening not made national/unrestricted.

summary: Saudi Arabia restricted ordinary passenger arrivals through the King Fahd Causeway from Bahrain from late on 7 March 2020 as part of its COVID-19 response. Commercial trucks and specially authorised humanitarian returns were excepted. On 22–23 July, Saudi citizens returning from Bahrain, with immediate family and domestic staff, were allowed to enter without prior authorisation; other travel restrictions continued under separate rules.

verification.notes: Explicit March 7 timing prevails over later March 8 rounding; July return-cohort policy relaxation only.

summary: Türkiye restricted ordinary road movement at Habur–Ibrahim Khalil on the Iraqi border from 1 March 2020 to limit COVID-19 transmission. Freight continued through exchanges of trailers, containers and drivers, while Turkish drivers could not normally take their own trucks into Iraq until 19 August. Türkiye had granted freight-driver permission earlier, on 4 June; passengers were also travelling under differentiated permit and health rules by mid-September, without a precise date for their first return.

verification.notes: Cargo continuation and two-sided driver permission distinguished; later passenger observation not exact reopening.

summary: Oman barred most foreign passenger entry from 17 March 2020 to limit COVID-19 transmission, initially exempting Gulf Cooperation Council citizens. From noon on 18 March it restricted entry to Omanis and prohibited their departure. Guidance published by 1 October allowed conditional resident returns and overseas departures, but tourist visas remained suspended and ordinary land access was still restricted; these changes do not establish a general reopening of every crossing.

verification.notes: Successive entry/departure policies and conditional October guidance retained; supersession not reopening.

summary: Jordan closed the Jaber–Nassib crossing with Syria to ordinary commercial traffic on 13 August 2020 following COVID-19 concerns. It granted special admission to trucks stranded between the crossings on 12 September, before general commercial traffic resumed on 27 September. Reopening used health-controlled cargo transfers to limit contact, while restrictions on ordinary passenger travel continued separately.

verification.notes: Observed freight restoration retained with stranded-truck exception; passenger chronology separate.

summary: Saudi Arabia temporarily suspended passenger entry through its land and sea ports in late December 2020 following concern about a new coronavirus variant. The initial one-week restriction was extended for another week and formally lifted at 11:00 on 3 January 2021. Goods, supply chains and emergency categories were excepted, while origin-specific health conditions and the separate restrictions on Saudi citizens travelling abroad remained.

verification.notes: Formal entry ban and lifting distinguished from outward-citizen restrictions and actual gate clocks.

summary: Kuwait closed its borders late on 21 December 2020 in response to the international COVID-19 situation and concern over a new variant. Nuwaiseeb reopened on 2 January 2021 for Kuwaiti citizens returning from Saudi Arabia, with limited daytime operating hours. That return arrangement does not establish unrestricted reopening for other nationalities, other land crossings or commercial freight.

verification.notes: Scoped returning-citizen operation from 09:00 Jan 2 retained; no blanket cargo claim.

summary: Oman ordered its land crossings closed from 18 January 2021 because of COVID-19 and repeatedly extended the restrictions. Trucks and time-limited returns by Omani citizens were excepted; specified cross-border workers gained permission in June. Conditional passenger entry from the UAE was authorised from 1 September, and Emirati tourist arrivals were reported by 15 September, but the evidence does not establish one uninterrupted closure or the same reopening date for all routes and travellers.

verification.notes: Sequential orders and exemptions not merged into continuous January–September operational interval.

summary: Iraqi authorities ordered the country’s land crossings closed around the parliamentary election on 10 October 2021 as part of election security measures. The announced window ran from the evening of 9 October to the morning of 11 October, although reports give conflicting starting times. The accounts do not establish when each crossing actually stopped or resumed traffic, or which travellers and goods were excepted.

verification.notes: Order-versus-implementation clock discrepancy retained without observed duration claim.

summary: Iran restricted travellers, including pilgrims, from crossing into Iraq during the unrest in Baghdad on 29–30 August 2022. The Interior Ministry linked the measure to the violence and Iraqi curfew. Permission to travel was restored on 30 August after tensions eased, but the reports do not establish simultaneous reopening at every crossing or the exact hours for which individual routes were closed.

verification.notes: Kept conflicting onset dates and permission-only endpoint; no assumed universal physical opening.

summary: Israel suspended Gaza’s exports through Kerem Shalom in early September 2023 after Israeli authorities said they had found explosives concealed in an outgoing consignment. The suspension was announced on 4 September for implementation the following day. Trucks carrying clothing and scrap iron were reported entering the Israeli side again on 10 September; the restriction concerned outgoing freight, rather than Gaza’s imports or passenger crossings.

verification.notes: Attributed explosives allegation; announcement/implementation bounds and actual export endpoint retained.

summary: Israel stopped permit-holding Palestinian workers from leaving Gaza through Erez–Beit Hanoun from 15 September 2023, initially for the Jewish holidays and then through security extensions. The crossing reopened for workers on 28 September. Medical and humanitarian applicants remained nominally eligible during the restriction, subject to approval, so the worker closure did not mean that all categories of passenger were prohibited.

verification.notes: Separated holiday start and security extensions; nominal medical permission not guaranteed passage.

summary: Direct aid entry into Gaza through the Israeli-controlled Kerem Shalom crossing stopped on 7 October 2023 and resumed on 17 December; earlier inspection arrangements had sent cargo through Rafah instead. Further aid-dispatch interruptions were reported in late December and after a 5 May 2024 closure, with one Jordanian food convoy entering on 9 May. These episodes had different causes and exceptions, and the return of limited aid did not restore normal trade or reliable distribution inside Gaza.

verification.notes: Preserved three distinct aid episodes; December intentional-restriction uncertainty and limited May convoy endpoint.

summary: Türkiye suspended traffic at crossings with northern Syria amid unrest and attacks on Turkish interests in early July 2024. Bab al-Hawa was reportedly closed late on 1 July, with passenger and lorry operations restored on 3 July. Commercial-truck movement at Bab al-Salam and al-Rai was reported restored on 8 July, but that did not establish the same reopening date for their passengers or permit holders.

verification.notes: Bab al-Hawa reported onset distinguished from July 2 notice; other gates truck-only endpoints.

summary: Israeli authorities closed Allenby–King Hussein Bridge and the Jordan River and Wadi Araba terminals after the shooting at Allenby on 8 September 2024. Passengers were using Allenby again by 10 September, although reports of intermittent access prevent a clear continuous closure period; some freight had returned by 23 September. The other two terminals were reported open by 12 September, without precise reopening times. Allenby connects Jordan with the occupied West Bank.

verification.notes: Retained contested passenger continuity and separate freight/other-terminal bounds; occupied territory described accurately.

summary: An Israeli air strike severed the road between Masnaa in Lebanon and Jdeidat Yabous in Syria on 4 October 2024, disrupting vehicle travel on a major route used by people fleeing the fighting. Pedestrians continued across the damaged road. Israel said the strike targeted weapons transfers; a Lebanese minister reported the road repaired and operational by 30 November, but repeated strikes and uncertain repair dates prevent a single continuous closure period being established.

verification.notes: Attributed weapons claim; vehicle/pedestrian distinction and bounded later restoration retained.

summary: An Israeli strike damaged the road at Qaa–Jousiyeh between Lebanon and Syria on 25 October 2024, blocking ordinary vehicle access. Further strikes and temporary movements followed, while pedestrians continued to cross. UNHCR observed cars and buses carrying Lebanese returnees from Syria on 1 December after repairs; this confirms restored access for those return journeys, but not an uninterrupted vehicle closure since October or an equivalent reopening date in the opposite direction.

verification.notes: Repeated strikes not collapsed; observed December return direction and pedestrian exception retained.

summary: Jordan restricted outward passenger and goods traffic through Jaber into Syria on 6 December 2024 as the Syrian government collapsed, while allowing Jordanian citizens and trucks to return. Freight permission was restored on 18 December, although some earlier truck movements were reported. From 25 May 2025, Jordanians using public transport could travel to Syria without prior approval, subject to security exclusions; the waiver did not generally cover private vehicles or mark the first passenger crossing.

verification.notes: Preserved outward direction, return exceptions, freight permissions and public-transport-only later waiver.

summary: Iraq announced the closure of Al-Qaim–Al Bukamal on 8 December 2024 following the fall of Syria’s government, citing border security. Regular passenger and commercial traffic resumed on 14 June 2025 after joint security assessments. The intervening restriction allowed exceptions, including Iraqi citizens returning with valid identification, humanitarian movements, stranded trucks and the repatriation of Syrian soldiers, so the crossing was not sealed to all movement throughout.

verification.notes: Regular-service endpoint separated from December exceptional access and repatriations.

summary: Israel stopped humanitarian and commercial supplies entering Gaza through its controlled crossings on 2 March 2025, presenting the measure as pressure for a new ceasefire and hostage-release arrangement. Limited humanitarian aid began crossing again on 19 May. This was a partial restart: fuel and other goods remained restricted, and permission for aid to enter did not ensure its collection or delivery to people inside Gaza.

verification.notes: Attributed political purpose; actual limited entry distinguished from permission and distribution.

summary: Israeli authorities restricted Allenby–King Hussein Bridge after the attack on 18 September 2025, disrupting passengers and the route used by aid convoys from Jordan to Gaza. Passenger access was reported restored by 22 September, but accounts of a brief earlier opening leave the uninterrupted closure period uncertain. Back-to-back food convoys resumed on 10 December; other commercial traffic and government-to-government aid convoys did not necessarily share that reopening.

verification.notes: Contested passenger sequence preserved separately from supported food-convoy interval.

summary: Israeli authorities ordered Allenby–King Hussein Bridge closed to passengers again from 24 September 2025, following a brief reopening after the earlier attack. Bus services operated for about two and a half hours on 26 September before another closure, and passenger movement was reported again on 28 September. Freight restrictions continued separately; the evidence does not establish the motive for this later order or uninterrupted closure between these reported movements.

verification.notes: No inferred political or security motive; brief bus operation and later reported restoration retained.

summary: Israel suspended Gaza crossings and coordinated movements on 28 February 2026 during wider regional hostilities. Kerem Shalom reopened for limited fuel and aid entry on 3 March, with fuel trucks documented entering from that date. Other crossings and transfers remained restricted, including movements from the West Bank and Jordan, so this did not represent a general restoration of Gaza’s imports, medical evacuations or humanitarian access.

verification.notes: Kerem Shalom limited fuel/aid endpoint distinguished from other routes and movements.

summary: Iraqi authorities suspended several crossings with Iran on 12 September 2026 for a security and administrative review, while Zurbatiyah and Munthiriya remained open. Passenger entry at Sheeb and Shalamcheh was reported restored on 13 September, and commercial movement resumed at Mandali on 15 September and at Shalamcheh by 16 September. Cargo entering Iraq at Sheeb was still restricted on 16 September; its announced reopening was not confirmed in the available evidence.

verification.notes: Separate passenger and cargo chronology retained; Sheeb last confirmation not reopening.

summary: Iraq suspended passenger and goods movement at Sheeb–Chazabeh on the Iranian border on 21 October 2026. Government officials cited technical and logistical deficiencies, while border officials also referred to security checks and equipment to detect prohibited goods. The restriction was still reported on 25 October, when Maysan’s governor called for reopening because of effects on trade and medical access; the available evidence does not establish a subsequent reopening.

verification.notes: Latest closure observation explicitly dated; reopening and zero-traffic claims not inferred.

summary: Ordinary civilian and commercial access through Al-Qaim–Al Bukamal, between Iraq and Syria, was restricted during years of conflict, while government, military and some humanitarian movements were permitted. Officials formally reopened the crossing to travellers and trade on 30 September 2019. Reports disagree over when the earlier restrictions began and describe changing refugee exceptions, so they do not establish one continuous closure of all traffic across those years.

verification.notes: Endpoint-only permission retained; disputed 2011/2012 onset and changing refugee access not flattened.

summary: Algeria closed its land border with Morocco on 27 August 1994 during a dispute over visas and security. Ordinary land travel remained restricted throughout the study period, with reports still describing the border as closed in January 2026 and official travel advice confirming that status in October. Authorised exceptions, including a prisoner handover in August 2024, did not reopen the frontier to the travelling public.

verification.notes: Original visa/security dispute retained; dated later observations and exceptional handover not zero movement.

summary: Egypt kept Rafah largely closed to passengers after the Sinai attack of 24 October 2014, allowing occasional opening days for groups including registered patients, students and foreign-visa holders. More sustained passenger access began on 12 May 2018 and was subsequently extended for Ramadan. The earlier period included repeated temporary openings, while the later schedule still required registration and eligibility checks; neither amounted to unrestricted passage.

verification.notes: Intermittent regime and sustained May 12 start distinguished from May 17 announcement.

summary: Libyan authorities reclosed Ras Jedir on the Tunisian border on 15 July 2018, hours after a brief reopening during disputes over fuel, subsidised goods, smuggling controls and travellers’ treatment. The checkpoint reopened on 1 September. Protesters still obstructed the approach road on the Tunisian side, however, so reopening the gate did not immediately restore access along the whole route.

verification.notes: Selected reclosure spell clearly identified; gate opening distinguished from continuing roadblock.

summary: Morocco stopped processing commercial consignments at Melilla–Beni Enzar in early August 2018, with a government spokesperson linking the decision to developing trade through Nador port. A trial aluminium shipment crossed from Melilla into Morocco on 27 January 2023. That experimental export was the first documented restoration of this customs route, rather than unrestricted two-way commercial reopening; passenger travel followed a separate set of restrictions.

verification.notes: Avoided inferred sovereignty motive; experimental one-way endpoint and slight onset discrepancy preserved through approximate phrasing.

summary: Egypt stopped passengers leaving Gaza through Rafah on 7 January 2019 after Palestinian Authority staff withdrew amid their dispute with Hamas. Entry from Egypt into Gaza continued on five days each week. Urgent cases were allowed to leave Gaza on 29 January, ending the documented outward stoppage for that group, but the date when ordinary outward travel fully resumed remains uncertain.

verification.notes: PA–Hamas context not asserted as formal Egyptian justification; urgent-only endpoint and inward operation retained.

summary: Libyan authorities suspended ordinary travel and goods movement at Ras Jedir overnight on 23–24 October 2019 during a dispute over delays and travellers’ treatment. People returning to their own country and ambulances were excepted. Libya’s Interior Ministry confirmed passenger traffic had resumed at midday on 7 November, following bilateral discussions; that confirmation does not establish unrestricted restoration of every goods category.

verification.notes: Kept overnight onset bounds and returning-citizen/ambulance exceptions; no fabricated earlier November 1 reopening.

summary: Morocco and Spain restricted ordinary passenger movement at Ceuta and Melilla in March 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic, with the Moroccan closure taking effect on 13 March. Initial exceptions allowed Spanish nationals to leave Morocco. Passenger crossings reopened on 17 May 2022 for EU residents and travellers authorised to enter the Schengen area, following improved bilateral relations; cross-border workers and commercial customs were handled through separate later arrangements.

verification.notes: Precise March 13 ordinary onset; initial exceptions and staged May eligibility retained.

summary: Algeria and Tunisia restricted ordinary passenger travel across their land border from 17 March 2020 to contain COVID-19. Freight and emergency passenger movements continued. Cars were observed crossing again on 15 July 2022 as nine posts reopened, ending the ordinary-travel restriction; the long interval should not be read as a complete halt to every traveller or shipment.

verification.notes: Ordinary passengers distinguished from emergency access and continuing freight.

summary: Egyptian and Palestinian authorities kept Rafah closed to passengers from 15 May 2020 as part of COVID-19 controls, while goods continued to enter Gaza through separate commercial arrangements. Passengers crossed in both directions during a temporary opening beginning on 11 August. The three-day window ended this passenger stoppage but did not establish a lasting return to normal daily travel.

verification.notes: Temporary August 11 window and freight exception retained.

summary: Civilian protesters obstructed the Guerguerat road through the disputed Western Sahara buffer strip to Mauritania on 21 October 2020, stopping passenger and freight traffic. Moroccan forces cleared the blockade on 13 November, and trucks were reported moving in both directions on 14 November. The territorial dispute and the parties’ competing claims formed the context; the evidence does not identify every protester’s affiliation or the first restored passenger journey.

verification.notes: Observed civilian blockade and actual truck endpoint; disputed claims not endorsed.

summary: Libya and Tunisia restricted ordinary passenger travel at Ras Jedir in July 2021 during the COVID-19 Delta wave. The closure was announced on 8 July and was reported operating by 9 July, with exceptions for stranded Libyans returning home and humanitarian departures. Passengers were observed crossing again on 17 September under health protocols; an earlier reopening announcement had not restored access, and the same operational endpoint is not established for Dhehiba–Wazin.

verification.notes: Retained onset bounds, humanitarian/return exceptions, failed August announcement and gate-specific actual endpoint.

summary: Rafah closed to passengers after strikes on 10 October 2023 during the Gaza war. Aid trucks began entering from Egypt on 21 October, but passenger exits did not resume until 1 November, when selected wounded Palestinians and foreign-passport holders were allowed into Egypt. That limited evacuation did not restore ordinary passenger travel, and the aid and passenger restrictions therefore had different endings.

verification.notes: Passenger exit and aid entry endpoints distinctly explained; no unsupported precise ordering actor.

summary: Ras Jedir closed to ordinary public traffic on 18–19 March 2024 after clashes between Libyan government security forces and local armed groups during an anti-smuggling deployment. Limited medical, humanitarian and diplomatic movements were permitted in June, with uneven implementation on the two sides. Ministers formally reopened the checkpoint on 1 July; that ceremony establishes restored public permission rather than the exact timing of unrestricted traffic.

verification.notes: Bounded cross-side onset, attributed anti-smuggling purpose and uneven June exceptions retained.

summary: Medical evacuations through Rafah from Gaza to Egypt stopped after Israeli forces took control of the Gaza side of the crossing on 7 May 2024. Patients began leaving through Rafah again on 1 February 2025 under the ceasefire arrangements, with children documented entering Egypt. Evacuations through other routes had a separate history, and the limited medical reopening did not restore unrestricted passenger, goods or aid movement through Rafah.

verification.notes: Route-specific medical closure; February actual passage not January mission deployment.

summary: Medical evacuation through Rafah stopped on 18 March 2025 when renewed hostilities closed the crossing and the EU border mission paused its operations. Medical departures from Gaza to Egypt resumed on 2 February 2026 under a controlled passenger arrangement. Other evacuation routes and returning passengers followed different timelines, so this interval concerns medical exits through Rafah rather than every movement into or out of Gaza.

verification.notes: Medical-only quantified period distinguished from controlled returnees and other routes.

summary: Medical evacuations and controlled returnee movements through Rafah were suspended on 28 February 2026 amid regional security escalation. The EU border mission resumed operations on 19 March, when medical passengers left Gaza for Egypt and returnees entered Gaza. Those observed journeys establish the restart of these limited passenger services, but do not establish that every form of movement or cargo had been stopped and restored together.

verification.notes: Actual passenger movement corroborates mission timeline; exact shutdown issuer not invented.

summary: Protesters from Ben Guerdane blocked the approach road to Ras Jedir at El Kaitoun on the evening of 14 March 2026, turning back Tunisian and Libyan vehicles in both directions. They alleged mistreatment and detention of Tunisian traders. Travellers, traders and ambulances were affected until traffic resumed at dawn on 15 March; this was an overnight road blockade, rather than a two-day checkpoint closure.

verification.notes: Attributed grievances and under-24-hour scope retained; no ambulance exemption invented.

summary: Ordinary passenger movement through Ras Jedir stopped on 15 March 2020 as Tunisia and Libya introduced COVID-19 restrictions. Libya’s separate closure order preserved screened returns by stranded Libyan citizens. Travellers were observed crossing Ras Jedir again on 14 November under bilateral reopening arrangements; Dhehiba–Wazin was also formally reopened, although the available accounts do not independently establish its first passenger movements.

verification.notes: Contemporary March 15 onset takes priority; separate Libyan order and observed/formal endpoints distinguished.

summary: Libyan authorities restricted ordinary passage at Ras Jedir in September 2017 after protesters in Ben Guerdane obstructed Libyan vehicles during a dispute linked in reporting to anti-smuggling enforcement. Ambulances and travellers returning home remained excepted. Vehicle traffic resumed on 25 September; accounts place the start on 17 or 18 September and give differing explanations involving protests, organisation of the crossing and competing border-agency powers.

verification.notes: Conflicting onset and motives retained without selecting an unsupported exclusive cause.

summary: Ordinary passenger travel at Ghadames–Debdeb, between Libya and Algeria, remained restricted during preparations for reopening in 2023 and was still reported closed in August 2024 for security reasons. Commercial traffic was already using the crossing, while a proposed December 2023 passenger reopening had been postponed. Earlier exceptional departures and incomplete records leave the start of the current passenger stoppage uncertain; later reopening preparations do not establish that ordinary passengers actually resumed crossing.

verification.notes: Gate-specific passenger restriction separated from commercial access and other gates’ historical exceptions.

summary: Libya closed entry and exit at its two main land crossings with Tunisia during the night of 12 May 2025, as fighting in Tripoli prompted people to leave the city. Traffic was reported moving normally in both directions again from 11:00 on 13 May. The official reason for the short closure and the treatment of individual passenger and freight categories were not established.

verification.notes: Fighting presented as context, not proved motive; overnight duration and two-way restoration retained.

summary: Egypt stopped ordinary passenger processing at Rafah on 26 November 2020, after a short period of passenger passage earlier that week. Goods imports and a small number of authorised entries into Gaza continued. A temporary two-way passenger opening began on 1 February 2021, followed by a regular five-day schedule from 9 February; the specific reason for the November reclosure remains unestablished.

verification.notes: First temporary reopening used; cargo and exceptional entry distinguished; pandemic motive not invented.

summary: Gaza’s Hamas-led authorities restricted access through Arba-Arba, the checkpoint leading to Erez, on 26 March 2017 after the killing of a Hamas figure. Entry was restored in stages on 26–27 March, while outward restrictions continued with changing exemptions, including differences between female and male medical patients. The Interior Ministry announced removal of the exit restrictions on 6 April; goods movement through Kerem Shalom was not affected.

verification.notes: Gaza-side control distinguished from Israeli permits; changing directions and announced ending retained.

summary: Israel imposed additional restrictions on goods through Kerem Shalom on 9 July 2018, saying it was responding to incendiary kites and balloons launched from Gaza. Exports and most imports stopped, while food, medicines and fodder remained permitted and fuel and gas faced changing rules. The additional ordinary-goods restrictions ended on 15 August, without ending the wider blockade or every control on Gaza’s trade.

verification.notes: Attributed rationale; stable non-exempt goods scope and underlying blockade distinction preserved.

summary: Israel closed Erez to ordinary passengers and Kerem Shalom to ordinary goods traffic on 25 March 2019 following rocket fire and escalating fighting. Urgent humanitarian movements remained permitted. Both crossings reopened on 31 March after relative calm returned, ending this additional restriction while the underlying blockade and permit requirements continued.

verification.notes: Additional non-exempt crossing closure distinguished from baseline restrictions and humanitarian exceptions.

summary: Israel restricted ordinary passengers at Erez and ordinary goods at Kerem Shalom from 4 May 2019 during an escalation in fighting with Gaza. Specific international travellers and fuel for the Gaza Power Plant were excepted, and the period also overlapped Israeli Memorial and Independence holidays. Both crossings resumed ordinary permitted operation on 12 May; the episode was not eight uninterrupted days of active fighting or a halt to all traffic.

verification.notes: Documented international-traveller/fuel exceptions and holiday overlap preserved.

summary: Iraqi authorities closed Shalamcheh to passengers travelling into Iran on 16 November 2019, reportedly at Iran’s request during protests following fuel-price increases. Goods and commercial trade were not affected. Passenger travel from Iraq into Iran resumed on 23 November; although reports referred to travellers of both nationalities, they do not separately establish when passage in the reverse direction was restored.

verification.notes: Nationality not confused with direction; trade exception and Iran-request attribution retained.

summary: Yemen’s internationally recognised government ordered a complete shutdown of al-Wadea on the Saudi border on 8 April 2020 as a COVID-19 precaution, extending earlier restrictions that had still allowed freight. Commercial trucking resumed on 12 April. Passenger restrictions continued after that reopening, so the four-day interruption concerns the additional halt to freight rather than the longer ban on ordinary travellers.

verification.notes: Commercial shutdown isolated from longer passenger regime; no directional claim beyond evidence.

summary: Israel restricted most goods entering Gaza through Kerem Shalom from 11 August 2020, saying it was responding to incendiary balloons. Humanitarian equipment was exempt, while fuel initially remained permitted and later faced its own restrictions. Crossing restoration is best supported on 1 September following a ceasefire agreement, although one later account gives 31 August; passenger access through Erez remained a separate issue.

verification.notes: Stable non-humanitarian goods scope; fuel changes and one-day endpoint disagreement retained.

summary: Israeli restrictions at Erez prevented Palestinian patients from leaving Gaza for treatment from 11 May 2021 during the hostilities. A life-saving-treatment exception was introduced on 25 May, but wider medical access remained restricted and the first physical passage under that exception is not precisely identified. Earlier aid deliveries through Kerem Shalom and access for international personnel did not restore access for these patients.

verification.notes: Patient-specific phase and policy relaxation retained; unrelated humanitarian movements not used as endpoints.

summary: Kurdistan Regional Government authorities closed Semalka–Fishkhabour after protests and clashes in mid-December 2021, disrupting trade between Iraqi Kurdistan and northeast Syria. Commercial traffic resumed on 24–25 January 2022, initially under limited arrangements, while previous passenger procedures were announced restored on 27 January. Some groups, including newlywed women seeking family reunification, remained excluded later, so the commercial reopening did not establish unrestricted passenger access.

verification.notes: Bounded onset/trade endpoint and uneven later passenger access retained.

summary: Israel extended restrictions on Gaza workers using Erez on 24 April 2022, citing rocket fire after an earlier Passover closure. Ordinary permit-holding workers could not leave for jobs in Israel, while patients, foreigners and selected businesspeople were excepted. The additional worker restriction ended on 26 April; the preceding holiday closure and continuing permit controls are separate from this episode.

verification.notes: Security extension only; exceptions and April 24 source priority retained.

summary: Israel kept Erez closed to affected Gaza exit-permit holders from 6 May 2022 after the Elad attack, extending a closure that had been scheduled to end after Memorial and Independence holidays. Permit-holding workers were allowed to return through the crossing on 15 May. The additional restriction affected workers, merchants and other passengers, but the evidence does not reconstruct every exception or remove the continuing permit requirements.

verification.notes: May 6 extension, not routine holiday start; exception inventory explicitly limited.

summary: Israel stopped movement through Erez and Kerem Shalom on 2 August 2022 for security reasons, before the 5–7 August fighting. Limited humanitarian passenger access and initial cargo movement resumed on 8 August, including observed fuel deliveries. Previously authorised non-humanitarian passengers, including workers, returned under the earlier access arrangements on 9 August; existing permit restrictions remained in force.

verification.notes: Partial August 8 and ordinary authorised August 9 endpoints distinguished; overlapping periods not added.

summary: Israel closed Erez and Kerem Shalom on 9 May 2023 during the escalation in fighting with Gaza, interrupting passenger travel and essential goods supplies. Previously authorised goods, including fuel, began returning gradually through Kerem Shalom on 14 May after the ceasefire. That goods reopening does not establish unrestricted trade or the first actual journey by every passenger category through Erez.

verification.notes: Documented goods endpoint used; passenger announcement not promoted to observed universal restoration.

summary: Commercial traffic at Semalka–Fishkhabour stopped on 11 May 2023 amid a dispute between the Kurdistan Regional Government and northeast Syria’s administration. Reports identify a separate interruption to humanitarian organisations later in May. Commerce was reported operating again on 5 June under existing crossing procedures, while passenger and humanitarian access remained selective; the reopening did not establish unrestricted daily travel in every direction.

verification.notes: Commercial and NGO onsets separated; June 5 operation prioritised over earlier narrower reopening plan.

summary: Türkiye barred Turkish-registered trucks from driving directly into Syria through Öncüpınar–Bab al-Salama during the civil war, with the restriction reported to date from 2011. Goods continued across the border after being transferred to Syrian trucks. Direct entry permission was announced for 4 March 2019 and trucks were observed crossing by 5 March, subject to customs documents and drivers accepting the journey’s risks.

verification.notes: Vehicle restriction not goods embargo; year-only onset and permission-to-observation endpoint bounds retained.

summary: Türkiye restricted non-essential commercial goods entering Syria through Cilvegözü–Bab al-Hawa in early August 2017 after Hayat Tahrir al-Sham took control of the area. Humanitarian supplies, food, medicine and hygiene goods remained permitted. Commercial restrictions were lifted on 18 October except for cement, while civilian passage remained restricted; this was a separate episode from the July fighting-related road blockade.

verification.notes: Essential-goods and continuing cement/passenger restrictions distinguished; separate July episode not merged.

summary: Iraqi protesters blocked Safwan on the Kuwaiti border on 14 July 2018 during demonstrations over jobs and public services in Basra. A military officer reported that the morning obstruction had been cleared and commercial traffic restored that afternoon. Later reporting again described the crossing as closed, but did not establish when a new stoppage began, so the initial same-day blockade cannot be treated as continuous with it.

verification.notes: First same-day commercial reopening retained despite later unreconciled closed observation.

summary: Protesters blocked Safwan–Abdali between Iraq and Kuwait during the night of 20 November 2019, interrupting passenger and commercial movements in both directions. Traffic resumed early on 21 November after they withdrew. The local sit-in expressed solidarity with Baghdad’s protesters and opposition to political-party control, but the crossing itself was blocked for only a few hours, rather than throughout the longer protest.

verification.notes: Overnight gate obstruction separated from multi-day sit-in; local demands attributed.

summary: Lebanon restricted incoming land passengers from 18 March 2020 because of COVID-19, while Syria introduced its own entry rules and freight continued. Citizen returns, diplomatic travel and other exceptions changed over time, with conditional passenger arrangements at Masnaa and Abboudieh announced in March 2021. Syria eased entry for Lebanese nationals on 13 December 2021, but these different permissions do not establish one uninterrupted two-way closure or a single general reopening date.

verification.notes: Direction/nationality policies kept distinct; observations and policy easing not stitched into continuous closure.

summary: Yemen’s internationally recognised government ordered land-port passenger restrictions in March 2020 to prevent COVID-19, while exempting commercial and humanitarian freight. An initial stoppage at al-Wadea interrupted pilgrims and residents returning from Saudi Arabia overnight on 16–17 March, before they were admitted again. Subsequent restrictions and special return permissions continued through May and June, so the evidence describes changing access rules rather than a single continuous ban on every passenger.

verification.notes: Initial under-24-hour operation separated from national order and later return exceptions.

summary: Jordan closed Jaber–Nassib to goods and passengers on 31 July 2021 because of the deteriorating security situation around Daraa in Syria. Freight resumed on 4 August using cargo transfers between vehicles. Broader passenger and direct-vehicle access eased on 29 September, but some merchant trips had already occurred, so that later change does not establish that every passenger had been continuously excluded since July.

verification.notes: Four-day cargo phase and later vehicle/passenger easing separated; merchant exceptions preserved.

summary: Israeli strikes damaged the bridge and immigration facilities at Arida between Lebanon and Syria during the night of 26–27 November 2024, interrupting passenger travel. Limited access for Lebanese nationals returning from Syria was restored by 1–2 December, with manual processing because systems remained damaged. This was a one-way return arrangement, rather than confirmation that the crossing had regained its full capacity or ordinary operation for all travellers.

verification.notes: Bounded strike and reopening dates; returnee-only one-way endpoint and systems damage retained.

summary: Renewed Israeli strikes damaged Arida on 6 December 2024, and Lebanese authorities closed crossings other than Masnaa for travellers’ safety. Some unspecified access was reported later in December, and pedestrians could enter Syria by early January. Syrian and Lebanese passengers resumed using private vehicles on 3 June 2025, while goods trucks still could not use the temporary route; the intervening exceptions prevent a claim of six months without any movement.

verification.notes: Intervening December/January access prevents continuous all-traffic interval; June passenger-vehicle scope only.

summary: Syria required foreign trucks making domestic deliveries to transfer their loads to Syrian vehicles in February 2026, while allowing escorted transit. A reciprocal arrangement for Lebanese and Syrian trucks at Masnaa–Jdeidat Yabous began on 13 February, with exceptions for specified cargoes and stranded vehicles. The trial was extended, and transshipment measures were still discussed as current in May; goods could continue moving even where the foreign truck itself could not enter.

verification.notes: Direct-vehicle prohibition distinguished from goods closure; scheduled expiry and later discussion not repeal.

summary: Syrian authorities briefly suspended passenger departures towards Lebanon at Jdeidat Yabous on 4 March 2026 following a warning of a possible strike. Arrivals remained permitted for Syrians fleeing Lebanon. Passenger traffic returned to normal later that day, reported around noon or early afternoon; the accounts do not establish the exact duration and do not describe a two-way closure.

verification.notes: Outbound-only scope, incoming escape exception and same-day timing disagreement retained.

summary: Lebanese and Syrian authorities evacuated Masnaa–Jdeidat Yabous after an Israeli strike warning on 4 April 2026, bringing ordinary passenger, freight and administrative activity almost to a halt. Normal traffic was reported again on 9 April after diplomatic contacts. The restriction was precautionary: the available monitoring reported no strike on this crossing, and some marginal or exceptional passage cannot be ruled out.

verification.notes: Threat not physical strike; near-total qualification and separate March episode preserved.

summary: Kuwait temporarily shut Abdali–Safwan after drone damage in late July 2026, describing the measure as precautionary. Passenger and commercial traffic were observed moving again on 26 July. Accounts differ between an official two-day shutdown and one traveller’s three-day wait, leaving the exact start uncertain; the reporting relays allegations about responsibility for the attack without independently establishing who carried it out.

verification.notes: Attack date not substituted for closure start; differing waits and allegations clearly attributed.

summary: Israel announced an unusually extended holiday restriction on Palestinian crossings in October 2017, citing security concerns following the Har Adar attack. At Erez, recorded business-category passengers stopped crossing on 4–7 October, returned on 8–10 October, and stopped again on 11–14 October before passage resumed on 15 October. Medical and other exceptional categories crossed at different times, so the evidence does not describe one eleven-day halt to all passengers.

verification.notes: Actual business-category phases replace broad announced-window narrative; other categories and non-operating days retained.

summary: Iran restricted Arbaeen pilgrims departing through Khosravi towards Iraq in early October 2019 because unrest and curfew in Baghdad obstructed their route. Reports place the suspension on 2–3 October and the reopening on 6–7 October, with a group of pilgrims documented departing by 7 October. Chazzabeh reportedly reopened earlier; freight, returning travellers and the physical sealing of the entire gate are not established by these accounts.

verification.notes: Pilgrim-route restriction rather than total gate seal; two-crossing endpoints not merged.

summary: Iranian authorities stopped Iranian and transit trucks driving directly into Iraq through Mehran on 30 October 2019 amid unrest and safety concerns. Goods could still be delivered to Iraqi trucks at the border terminal. The direct-entry restriction was reported continuing on 3 November, but its end is unclear: later references to a general reopening do not distinguish foreign trucks from cargo transferred between vehicles.

verification.notes: Vehicle ban distinguished from transferred cargo; November 3 confirmation not endpoint.

summary: Israel restricted ordinary passenger and goods traffic at Erez and Kerem Shalom during the fighting of 12–14 November 2019. Some Erez passengers were admitted exceptionally, and fuel had a separate access history. Previously eligible traffic was reported restored by 17 November, after the intervening weekend; the accounts therefore do not establish five continuous days of conflict-related closure for every category.

verification.notes: Conflict days and later operation bound distinguished; non-fuel goods and passenger exceptions preserved.

summary: Moroccan authorities restricted ordinary passenger and private-vehicle travel at Guerguerat from 18 March 2020 to limit COVID-19 transmission, while professional freight traffic remained permitted. Passenger permission was restored on 9–10 November 2021, although the first actual journeys are not precisely identified. The crossing links Moroccan-administered Western Sahara with Mauritania, and the separate protest blockade on the same road followed a different chronology.

verification.notes: Disputed-territory description and formal passenger endpoint maintained; freight/protest scopes separate.

summary: Moroccan authorities again restricted ordinary passenger travel through Guerguerat on 30 November 2021 because of the Omicron coronavirus variant, while goods transport continued. Mauritanian nationals were allowed to return to Mauritania from 8 December, but other ordinary travellers remained restricted. Broader passenger movement in both directions resumed on 4 April 2022 under health conditions, ending this renewed episode rather than a continuous closure dating back to 2020.

verification.notes: November opening prevents two-year continuity claim; nationality/direction return exception retained.

summary: Saudi authorities restricted Yemen-bound SUVs and heavy equipment at al-Wadea from the evening of 5 July 2018. More than fifty qualifying SUVs entered Yemen on 9 July after talks, with owners required to accompany their vehicles and provide documents; Shas and Hilux vehicles remained excluded. Reports of some earlier passage leave the first reopening uncertain, and the official purpose of the restriction was not established.

verification.notes: Conditional vehicle endpoint and unreconciled July 6 access retained; no invented motive.

summary: Iraq stopped passengers leaving through Sheeb for Iran on 16 November 2019 at Iran’s request during protests over fuel prices. Goods and trade continued through the crossing. The Iraqi Border Ports Commission reported travel into Iran restored on 25 November after a nine-day interruption; its statement does not establish an equivalent restriction or reopening date for passengers travelling in the opposite direction.

verification.notes: Outgoing passenger direction and continuing trade explicit; one official reporting lineage acknowledged in evidence.

summary: Iraq barred Iranian passenger entry through land crossings from 20 February 2020 because of COVID-19, then extended the restriction to non-Iraqi arrivals from Iran. Iraqi returnees and imported goods were excepted. Later permissions included approved pilgrim caravans in June 2022 and eligible individual or group pilgrims in July, alongside earlier visa-based exceptions; these limited changes do not establish a single uninterrupted ban or general reopening for all foreign passengers.

verification.notes: Initial/successor policies separated from pilgrim exceptions and unrelated August security closure.

summary: Saudi border authorities restricted Yemen-bound privately owned SUVs at al-Wadea during March 2021. Yemeni officials disputed the wider application of a request aimed at commercial pickups allegedly being diverted to fighting. More than one hundred vehicles were reported admitted on 25 April when owners were present, but the exact March start and any continuing exclusions for particular models or commercial vehicles remain uncertain.

verification.notes: Security allegation and disputed wider implementation attributed; conditional owner-present endpoint not universal.

summary: Iraq suspended passenger and commercial movement at Shalamcheh on 4 April 2026 after a strike hit the Iranian-side passenger hall. Passenger travel resumed later the same day, and an Iranian official reported pilgrim, trader and commercial activity restored by the evening. The precise freight interruption and conditions in each direction are not established, and the evidence does not independently identify responsibility for the strike.

verification.notes: Same-day passenger operation distinct from less precise freight reporting; attack attribution withheld.

summary: Protesters and armed actors obstructed the Libyan approach to Ras Jedir from the evening of 22 August 2024 amid disputes over commercial access and control of the crossing. Authorities cleared the route and passenger and ordinary-vehicle traffic was reported restored in both directions on 28 August, although one account described a shorter four-day stoppage. Freight restrictions and a separate official outbound suspension had different scopes; Dhehiba–Wazin remained an alternative route.

verification.notes: Explicit onset and conflicting shorthand retained; passenger route versus freight/official order distinguished.

summary: Israel prohibited its citizens from departing through Taba for Sinai on 10 April 2017, citing an imminent terrorist threat during Passover travel. Israeli citizens could still return, and foreign travellers were permitted to leave. The government extended the prohibition beyond its original planned expiry before restoring departure permission on 21 April; the first actual outbound crossing under that permission is not separately documented.

verification.notes: Citizenship/direction and exceptions preserved; government permission not observed first passage.

summary: Saudi Arabia restricted passenger arrivals by land from Kuwait and the UAE on 7 March 2020 as part of its COVID-19 response, directing ordinary entry towards approved airports while allowing commercial trucks under health controls. On 23 July, Saudi citizens, immediate family and domestic staff could return through land ports without prior authorisation. Earlier humanitarian and social exceptions remained distinct from this wider permission, which did not reopen every passenger category.

verification.notes: Kuwait/UAE scope only; citizen-family relaxation distinguished from all-passenger restoration.

summary: Israel prohibited ordinary departures by its citizens through Taba to Egypt from 18 March 2020 as a COVID-19 precaution. Outbound pedestrians were allowed to cross again on 30 March 2021 under a daily quota for vaccinated or recovered Israelis, with testing requirements. This limited reopening did not restore unrestricted vehicle travel, and restrictions on people returning to Israel followed a different chronology.

verification.notes: Outbound citizenship scope, March 18 onset and quota-limited pedestrian endpoint retained.

summary: Kuwait ordered land-entry restrictions for non-exempt foreign travellers from 24 February to 20 March 2021 because of COVID-19. Returning citizens with close relatives or domestic helpers, shipping personnel and neutral-zone workers were excepted. Later rules allowed accredited fully vaccinated travellers from 1 August, but the scheduled March expiry and later permission do not establish an uninterrupted February–August closure or the first actual journeys through land posts.

verification.notes: Scheduled initial window and endpoint-only later permission remain distinct; no continuous interval inferred.

summary: Tunisia stopped departures towards Libya at Ras Jedir on 5 January 2018 while armed factions disputed control of the Libyan post. Tunisian citizens returning from Libya were allowed through. Reports describe reopening on the afternoon of 6 January and restored activity by 7 January, leaving the exact resumption for outbound travellers uncertain; the restriction was not a complete ban on movement in both directions.

verification.notes: Outbound prohibition and returnee exception preserved; reopening bounds not narrowed.

summary: The King Fahd Causeway Authority briefly suspended vehicle traffic between Saudi Arabia and Bahrain early on 7 April 2026 following security warnings in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Province. Movement was reported restored later that day after a stoppage lasting several hours. A subsequent renewed suspension was a separate episode; the reports do not detail every vehicle category or any exemptions.

verification.notes: First same-day spell isolated from renewed closure; all decisive reports share authority source.

summary: The King Fahd Causeway Authority suspended vehicle traffic between Saudi Arabia and Bahrain again on 7 April 2026 after renewed regional security warnings. Normal vehicle movement in both directions was reported restored on 8 April. This followed an earlier same-day reopening, so the two suspensions cannot be combined into one uninterrupted closure, and the overnight dates alone do not establish that this second stoppage exceeded 24 hours.

verification.notes: Renewed episode and intervening access maintained; no >24-hour inference from dates.

summary: Yemeni authorities reportedly suspended services at Sarfait on the Omani border after an armed confrontation in Al Mahrah in early July 2025. Accounts place the interruption around 7–8 July and report reopening by 8–9 July, but disagree over the precise days. The reports cite preventive security concerns without independently establishing the alleged offences or affiliations involved, and do not specify how passengers and goods were treated.

verification.notes: Closure dates not derived from detention date; contested actor allegations and category gaps retained.

summary: Gaza-solidarity protesters obstructed Iraqi oil tankers heading to Jordan on the approach to Trebil in October 2023, with a declared ban reported on 25 October. Some tankers entered Jordan on 26 October and the final affected October deliveries were reported complete by 27 October, while other accounts still described obstruction. The evidence therefore indicates intermittent tanker disruption, rather than one continuous closure of the crossing to all goods and passengers.

verification.notes: Oil-tanker cohort and conflicting intermittent passage retained; delivery completion only bounds episode.

summary: Traders and other demonstrators blocked Shahn land port in Yemen’s Al Mahrah governorate on 6 March 2022 in protest against increased customs charges. Reporting describes disruption to commercial activity but does not establish passenger restrictions or the precise direction of affected trade. The protesters threatened to continue their sit-in, yet the available evidence does not show how long the crossing remained obstructed or when it reopened.

verification.notes: Protest actor rather than government order; threatened duration not actual continuity.

summary: Libyan authorities were reported to have closed their side of Ras Jedir on the Tunisian border on the morning of 11 April 2017 after armed clashes. The account does not identify the responsible agency or distinguish passenger and freight categories. A later second-hand reopening report gives a conflicting start date, leaving the end and duration of this particular interruption unconfirmed.

verification.notes: Onset-only accepted evidence and conflicting unconfirmed restoration preserved.

summary: Fires damaged Kerem Shalom during protests in May 2018, prompting Israeli and Palestinian authorities to announce closures for repairs. Goods entry into Gaza was interrupted after damage on 11 and 14 May, although selected humanitarian trucks passed on 13 May. Palletised goods resumed partially on 16 May and fuel entry on 17 May; these changing permissions do not establish a continuous complete halt to all goods or every fuel type.

verification.notes: Infrastructure-repair cause; humanitarian passage and separate goods/fuel endpoints retained.

summary: Libyan crossing authorities suspended ordinary services at Dhehiba–Wazin from 13 April 2018 while mourning the crossing commander’s death. Exceptional and urgent cases were still allowed through during the stoppage. Normal service was reported restored on 16 April, but the accounts do not itemise all passenger and freight categories or establish the exact closing and reopening hours.

verification.notes: Mourning purpose and urgent exceptions explicit; three calendar days not 72 measured hours.

summary: Protests and disputes around Dhehiba–Wazin disrupted passenger and goods access in August 2018, involving both the Libyan gate and the Tunisian approach road. The local mayor reported normal movement restored by 12 August after the road was secured. Accounts of an earlier gate closure, returning-national exceptions and some continuing traffic do not establish a single uninterrupted blockage or a precise first reopening date.

verification.notes: Gate versus road mechanisms and conflicting continuing access preserved; no invented August 8 onset interval.

summary: Libyan authorities restricted ordinary travel at Dhehiba–Wazin from 14:00 to 22:00 on 10 August 2023. Tunisians returning to Tunisia and Libyans returning to Libya were allowed to cross during the interruption. Traffic resumed that evening, but the reports give no reason for the measure and do not fully describe freight or third-country travellers; the reported stoppage lasted hours, rather than a whole day.

verification.notes: Reported eight-hour window and nationality-direction return exceptions retained; motive not invented.

summary: Commercial traffic at Dhehiba–Wazin was suspended on the Libyan side for a reported two days in December 2023, while ordinary passenger travel continued. Trade was reported restored on the morning of 30 December. The accounts do not identify the precise starting date, commodities affected, direction of trade or official reason, so the reported duration should not be converted into an exact 48-hour closure.

verification.notes: Passenger exemption and reported two-day duration retained without back-calculated onset.

summary: Egypt closed Rafah to passengers on 23 August 2021 without providing an official reason. Palestinians stranded in Egypt began returning to Gaza on 26 August, while outward passenger movement from Gaza to Egypt resumed on 29 August. The two directions therefore had different reopening dates; separate aid deliveries and commercial supplies through Salah Ad Din were not shown to be closed by these passenger measures.

verification.notes: Directional actual endpoints explicit; political context not invented as rationale.

summary: Israel closed Kerem Shalom to commercial entry into Gaza on 14 January 2018 while its military carried out an operation to destroy a tunnel, citing safety around the work. The route carried commercial goods, aid and fuel. It reopened on 16 January, according to subsequent reporting; the episode does not establish a passenger closure or the exact hours for which each type of consignment was stopped.

verification.notes: Tunnel-operation rationale attributed; actual January 16 goods reopening distinguished from prior plan.

summary: Israel stopped fuel deliveries through Kerem Shalom to Gaza’s sole power plant on the morning of 25 June 2019, saying it was responding to incendiary balloons. Deliveries resumed on 28 June, and the electricity supplier reported that renewed fuel supplies allowed another generator to operate. The interruption concerned that power-plant supply route, not every fuel user, other commercial goods or passenger travel.

verification.notes: Specific commodity/destination and actual supply restoration retained.

summary: Tunisian protesters obstructed the approach to Dhehiba–Wazin during the night of 13 February 2021, demanding that goods flows resume. Passenger and goods passage was reported restored on 14 February after the obstruction ended. The account describes several hours of disruption rather than a full-day closure, and does not specify every direction of travel or any permitted exceptions.

verification.notes: Approach blockade and short overnight duration explicit; no official policy inferred.

summary: Protests over trade and local development disrupted Ras Jedir and its Ben Guerdane approach during December 2016 and January 2017. Ordinary passenger and goods passage was blocked on 13–14 December, with emergencies and Libyans returning home excepted. Further interruptions followed amid repeated openings, and normal vehicle traffic was reported restored on 23 January; the earlier agreement of 17 January had not itself reopened the route.

verification.notes: Two interrupted phases and exceptions retained; protest campaign not equated to continuous closure.

summary: Young protesters blocked the road and locked gates at Dhehiba–Wazin on 24 April 2017, demanding jobs and development and expressing solidarity with the Kamour protest movement. The governor reported activity restored on the evening of 8 May after roughly two weeks. The accounts establish disruption to ordinary access but do not enumerate every affected passenger or freight category, direction or exemption.

verification.notes: Actual return of activity distinguished from meeting decision; actor demands supported.

summary: Protests over seized goods and threats against travellers disrupted Dhehiba–Wazin and its approach road in late November and early December 2017. Libyan authorities restricted ordinary passage, while returning nationals and some other groups were permitted through. Activity was reported restored by 7 December, but roadblocks, checkpoint restrictions and temporary access changed during the dispute, leaving no reliable common starting date for an uninterrupted closure.

verification.notes: Separate mechanisms and exceptions retained; completed-action December 7 bound not prospective source alone.

summary: Israel imposed additional restrictions on previously eligible passengers at Erez from 19 August 2018, attributing the decision to violence along the Gaza boundary. Urgent medical cases, international aid workers and foreign humanitarian representatives remained excepted. The crossing reopened for ordinary eligible passengers on 27 August after relative calm, while existing permit controls and the separate restrictions on goods through Kerem Shalom continued.

verification.notes: Non-exempt passenger scope and precise contemporary dates preferred over later three-week shorthand.

summary: Israel closed Erez to non-exempt passengers on 5 September 2018, initially citing repairs, and then extended the restriction as a stated response to vandalism. Patients, international organisations and some returning travellers were allowed through, while business and training passengers remained excluded. Officials confirmed reopening on 13 September; overlapping holiday closures and differing exceptions prevent an exact measure of every passenger’s operational delay.

verification.notes: Initial repair and punitive extension reasons attributed separately; formal restoration not measured throughput.

summary: Passenger services at Semalka–Fishkhabour were disrupted in June 2021 while the crossing administration cited new traveller procedures on the Iraqi Kurdistan side. Trade, some humanitarian organisations and certain travellers with foreign residency remained excepted. Selected services for brides, humanitarian cases and foreign or Iraqi residence holders resumed on 28 June, but conflicting reports of earlier closures and reopenings leave the start and continuity of the broader passenger restriction uncertain.

verification.notes: Unknown start and conflicting June 21/23 events preserved; specific returning cohorts only.

summary: Semalka’s administration announced that travellers holding Iraqi or Kurdistan Region residency would no longer be able to depart northeast Syria towards Iraqi Kurdistan after 6 September 2020. Other passenger groups and emergency cases followed different rules. By 29 November, officials described these residency holders as eligible to leave on three days each week, but the first enforcement and restoration dates were not documented, and no general trade closure was established.

verification.notes: Intended September 7 onset distinguished from publication; later cohort permission not operational endpoint.

summary: Officials formally reopened Rabia–al-Yarubiyah between Iraq and Syria to ordinary travellers and trade on 20 April 2026, after a prolonged but incompletely dated restriction; tanker exports from Iraq began on 1 May. UN humanitarian shipments had used the crossing earlier, so it was not continuously closed to all traffic. Those UN services ceased after their cross-border mandate was removed in January 2020, and the 2026 ordinary reopening does not establish restoration of that separate aid mechanism.

verification.notes: Ordinary formal reopening, observed tankers and UN mandate/service cessation kept separate.

summary: UN humanitarian convoys stopped using Bab al-Hawa from Türkiye into northwest Syria after the Security Council authorisation expired in July 2023. The first returning UN convoy crossed on 19 September following new consent arrangements. Earlier diplomatic permissions did not themselves restart deliveries, and the interruption concerns this UN service rather than all aid providers, commercial traffic or passengers using the crossing.

verification.notes: Actual convoy return distinguished from mandate expiry and consent; other services outside scope.

summary: Ordinary passage at Dhehiba–Wazin was interrupted during the night of 25 December 2017 and restored around noon on 26 December. A Tunisian customs spokeswoman cited security information, while a separate account linked the stoppage to traders’ complaints about goods seized by Libyan officials. Returning nationals were reportedly allowed through on the Libyan side; the competing explanations remain attributed, and the overnight interruption was not a full-day closure.

verification.notes: Alternative official/trader explanations and returning-national exception retained; separate late-December episode.
